title: Weekly links July 31: AI use in journal submissions and refereeing, what makes a top paper, lessons from the world, and more…
gist: A development-economics links roundup whose centerpiece is an Organization Science editorial study finding that fewer than 40% of submissions are now classified as low-AI-use and roughly a quarter appear mostly machine-written, with AI-drafted referee reports spreading in parallel and degrading review quality. Secondary items cover what separates a top-5 economics paper from an identical natural experiment, new applied-econometrics tooling, and a JDE call for papers on escaping the middle-income trap.

themes.theme: AI is flooding academic peer review

insights.claim: The editors of Organization Science report a large increase in journal submissions since the launch of ChatGPT, which they attribute to the falling cost of producing a manuscript.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Generative AI collapses the marginal cost of producing credentialed-looking content, so any gatekeeping institution paid in volunteer labor — journals, grant panels, sell-side research screening — faces a volume shock before it faces a quality shock.
insights.quote: the editors of the journal Organization Science noted the large increase in submissions their journal had received since ChatGPT was launched
insights.locator: I went to the SFSX conference this week

insights.claim: Fewer than 40% of submissions to Organization Science are now classified as low AI use, and about a quarter appear to be mostly written by AI, based on Pangram detection scores.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A hard, quantified penetration rate for AI-generated professional text inside a high-friction gatekept channel — a useful base rate for sizing how far AI drafting has spread into lower-friction commercial writing.
insights.quote: now less than 40% of all submissions are classified as low AI use, while about a quarter seem mostly written by AI

insights.claim: Papers with high detected AI use tend to be lower quality and are more likely to be desk-rejected, so the AI submission surge is concentrated in the bottom of the quality distribution rather than spread evenly.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: AI is expanding the tail of low-value output rather than lifting the mean — the same asymmetry to expect in AI-assisted content businesses, where volume rises but marginal quality falls.
insights.quote: They show that these tend to be lower quality and more likely to get desk-rejected.

insights.claim: Referees are increasingly using AI to write reviews, and AI-assisted reviews are harder to read, use more jargon, and cover a narrower evaluative range — weighted toward theory and away from data and context.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Quality control itself is being automated, which means the failure mode is not just more bad input but a screening layer that systematically stops checking the empirical parts — watch for the same blind spot in AI-run compliance and diligence workflows.
insights.quote: reviews that use AI are harder to read, use more jargon, and the reviews cover a more narrow evaluative range – more focused on theory, and less on data and context

insights.claim: Institutional incentives that tie careers to publication counts in specific journal lists are accelerating the flood of AI-written manuscripts and straining the volunteer labor pool that evaluates research.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The binding constraint is the incentive structure, not the technology — any system that rewards counted output over evaluated output will be arbitraged first and hardest by generative AI.
insights.quote: Institutional incentives—particularly when careers depend on publication counts in specific journal lists—appear to be accelerating this trend.

insights.claim: The Organization Science editors judge that AI is placing the peer-review system under stress that shows no signs of decreasing, framing the strain as structural rather than a transitional adjustment.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: If credentialing institutions are structurally impaired, the value of alternative verification and provenance layers rises — a tailwind for AI-detection and content-authenticity tooling.
insights.quote: In short, AI is placing the peer-review system under stress that shows no signs of decreasing

insights.claim: AI use detected in a paper's abstract is strongly correlated with AI use across the overall paper, making abstract-level screening a cheap and scalable proxy for full-document detection.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Cheap sampling-based detection is viable at scale, which lowers the cost of deploying AI-provenance screening across large document corpora.
insights.quote: showing in a subsample that AI use in abstract is strongly correlated with AI use in the overall paper

themes.theme: Positioning, not identification, makes a top-5 paper

insights.claim: Jason Fletcher compares his own work on NAFTA's impact on mortality with a contemporaneous paper exploiting the same natural experiment and reaching the same first-order result, and argues the other will land in a top-5 journal because of how it positions itself and the extras it adds.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Identification is a commodity; framing and generalizability are the scarce input — the same reason two analysts with identical data get paid very differently for the same call.
insights.quote: which he thinks will end up in a top 5 because of the way it positions itself and some of the extras it does
insights.locator: What turns a research question into a top 5 paper?

insights.claim: The specific moves that elevate an empirical paper are linking it to a broader and more general question in the literature, adding a welfare calculation, and reframing the presentation — not producing a different empirical result.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A reusable checklist for turning a narrow finding into a decision-relevant one: generalize the question, quantify the welfare or P&L stakes, and reframe.
insights.quote: This include positioning the paper in the literature to link to a broader and more general question, adding in a welfare calculation, and the way it frames.
insights.locator: What turns a research question into a top 5 paper?

insights.claim: Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham is curating recent theoretical econometrics papers from top journals and translating the main idea and the conditions under which each matters for applied researchers.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Method diffusion runs through curators, not journals — a low-cost way to track which estimators will start appearing in the empirical work that shapes policy consensus.
insights.locator: I really like this effort by Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham

insights.claim: Davide Viviano, Kaspar Wuthrich and Paul Niehaus have produced a plain-language summary of when multiple hypothesis testing adjustments are necessary and when they are not needed.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Directly relevant to anyone reading multi-outcome studies or backtests: knowing when correction is required separates a real effect from a mined one.
insights.locator: In VoxDev, Davide Viviano, Kaspar Wuthrich and Paul Niehaus

insights.claim: The Asian Development Bank Institute, with the Journal of Development Economics, is soliciting papers and research proposals for a conference and special issue on Escaping the Middle-Income Trap, with a 15 September 2026 deadline.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A leading development institution is formally organizing research around middle-income stagnation, signalling where the policy consensus on emerging-market growth ceilings will be reshaped over the next two years.
insights.quote: with a submission deadline of 15 September 2026
insights.locator: Call for papers: The Asian Development Bank Institute

insights.claim: Planet Money's Summer School is running a World Tour format built from archival excerpts, with an episode on China and building things and another on field experiments in Kenya and Nigeria featuring Tavneet Suri, including the YouWin! business plan competition.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Mainstream economics media is centering non-US development experiments and Chinese state capacity in building — a sign of where popular economic narrative is shifting.
insights.locator: Planet Money's Summer School is a great way
